newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. feels Sharif serious about talks with India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. feels Sharif serious about talks with India.

text.p: The United States believes Pakistan's Nawaz Sharif, who is heading for a landslide victory in national elections, is serious about resuming dialogue with India, a senior official said on Tuesday.

"I think that Nawaz Sharif has been saying very hopeful things about his intentions in terms of starting a dialogue with India," Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs, Robin Raphel, told reporters here.
Raphel held talks with senior Pakistan officials last month during a two-week South Asian swing that took in a meeting in Dhaka, Bangladesh with U.S. ambassadors to the region.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over Kashmir, since gaining independence from Britain in 1947.
The neighbours have not held official talks for over three years.
Pakistan has said it wants Kashmiris to be able to vote in a plebiscite to determine their future. India, which rules over two-thirds of the Himalayan region, says the issue is strictly internal.
India accuses Pakistan of providing armed support to the Kashmiri separatists, but Pakistan says it only provides moral and political support.
Raphel noted that Sharif, during his previous tenure as prime minister from 1990 to 1993, met with former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao several times.

"I think the combination of his own attitude on the political side plus his constituency in terms of the industrial and enterpreneurial class there and their desire to open trade links with India are very positive straws in the wind," she said.
Raphel said she had met with several Indian leaders including Farooq Abdullah, the chief minister of troubled Jammu and Kashmir state.
Abdullah took power in October after the first local polls in about a decade in the Himalayan state where an armed separatist revolt begun in 1990.
More than 20,000 people have died in the seven-year revolt, according to hospital and police sources.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda pledged to discuss the issue of autonomy for Kashmir before the local polls.
"It is the whole question of autonomy and how much, when, how and so on," Raphel said, adding it was not clear if autonomy discussions were under way.
"I think it needs to be sooner rather than later in order to take advantage of the window of opportunity that the (Kashmir) elections have provided."
